title: Cocoercivity does not give a quadratic residual rate for Douglas–Rachford splitting
shortTitle: An exact limit to a proposed splitting guarantee
oneLine: Small exact counterexamples refute a proposed squared-residual guarantee; the correct uniform worst-case order is inverse-linear, with carefully restricted scalar-step consequences.
abstract: Douglas–Rachford splitting tackles a coupled problem through simpler resolvent calculations. A conjecture proposed that cocoercivity of one operator, together with a convex subdifferential for the other, would give a uniform inverse-square bound on the squared update residual. This candidate refutes that statement using exact scalar and planar examples and proves that the correct uniform worst-case squared-residual order is inverse-linear for every fixed admissible parameter triple. Hinge-and-rotation witnesses also exclude an elementary finite-horizon repair considered in the paper. Additional results describe prescribed linear schedules and adaptive scalar-policy limits using credited classical and recent ingredients. An elementary corollary gives the exact linear-subclass infimum for scalars in the conventional open interval, without a nonlinear upper claim. These are fixed-point residual results, not objective-gap bounds or evidence of practical solver failure. The source paper's separate objective acceleration conjectures remain open. A bounded search located no earlier direct refutation; inaccessible full text leaves overlap of the scheduling synthesis unresolved.

narration:
When does a mathematical guarantee promise too much? This Evidence Press briefing concerns an unrefereed, AI-assisted research candidate about Douglas–Rachford splitting, a method that tackles a difficult problem through two simpler calculations.

A recent conjecture proposed a fast guarantee for the squared size of the method's updates. Roughly, doubling the iteration count should improve its worst-case bound by a factor of four, under the stated assumptions.

The paper gives two exact counterexamples. One works in a single real dimension. The other uses a two-dimensional rotation and does not require overrelaxation. Both obey the conjecture's actual conditions. Across the full stated class, the worst-case squared residual instead decreases at the order of one divided by the iteration count.

Why can this happen? The condition called cocoercivity controls a rotational component, but does not eliminate it. It is not the same as requiring a convex gradient.

There are important limits. The quantity studied is a fixed-point residual, not an objective gap or the distance to the solution. Each fixed rotational example can still converge geometrically. The worst-case construction changes with the number of iterations being tested. This is not a claim that practical solvers fail to converge.

The package also examines carefully restricted scalar-step choices and supplies exact hinge examples. Those scheduling results build on credited earlier mathematics; no historical-priority claim is made for that synthesis. One related full-text comparison remains unavailable.

The complete paper provides the assumptions, proofs, rational checks and remaining questions. Internal AI review and producer-side replay are not external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. The original paper's separate objective-value conjectures remain open.
